explanation: No single token type. It fires on many function words and punctuation (commas, colons, ' of' in 'Description of the Related Art', path separators like '/' or '_started'), seemingly at structural points right before a phrase continues. No consistent lexical or semantic trigger is visible.

A mixture. It fires on code tokens such as '__name__', indentation before '@Override public', '$_POST', 'function', '.length' and callback arguments, and also on scattered prose tokens like ' quite', 'back' in 'quarterback', ' blame' and 'Fixtures'. These share no clear common thread.

Fires on content nouns, or noun pieces, that name a technical or domain entity, usually in scientific or technical text: ' acid', 'magnet', ' complex', ' lead', 'ector', ' class', ' packet', ' polymer', ' peptide'. The noun is often the head of a noun phrase right after a modifier or determiner. Function words do not activate it.

Fires most reliably on ' with' in the license boilerplate 'use this file except in compliance with the License'. Beyond that it fires on scattered tokens: URL pieces, ' Sandy' and ' pose' repeated from earlier in the passage, 'Seq', and a date's leading space. These have no evident common meaning.

Heterogeneous. Triggers include empty parentheses '()' after a function name in prose or error messages, negations (' not', ''t'), ' I' after 'neither did', parts of abbreviations or acronyms ('GF', 'd' in F.Supp.2d, 'QM'), and closing quotes. No single concept covers them.

Fires on a wide variety of mostly function tokens (' to', ' of', commas, ' we', ' want', ' return', '="') across all genres, with no visible shared context. It looks like a diffuse, positional or syntactic unit.

Fires on the head noun or word of common fixed quantity and relation phrases: 'number' in 'the number of' or 'total number of', 'role' in 'key role', 'part' in 'integral/small part', and 'of' in 'because of'. It also fires on similar connective words like ' also' and ' only' in 'not the only'. The surrounding fixed-phrase context matters.

Fires on a scattered set of tokens. Some are the word completing fixed expressions ('safe to say', 'safe to assume', 'so as to', 'not only', 'not to mention', 'union all', 'can be'), and others are list items in enumerations (commas, digits, symbols in formulas or package lists). There is a weak fixed-phrase-completion theme but much noise.

Responds to context about duration or length, especially the words 'short' or 'long' appearing nearby. It fires on the following tokens: ' a' in 'for a few weeks' or 'for a period', 'a' in 'short message service (SMS). The', 'unsigned' after 'short' in C type declarations, and 'and' in 'novelettes and short stories'. The strongest cases have 'short' or 'long' in the immediate context.

A mixture. Its strongest triggers are tokens in code headers and boilerplate, such as license text (' the' in 'in the file', ' IMPLIED', ' ownership', ' to use'), import paths ('quarkus', 'fake') and court order headers. It also fires on random prose words ('wait for', 'is'). No single consistent trigger.

Fires on words inside software license and copyright header boilerplate (' regarding copyright ownership', 'bundled with', ' shall', 'Ltd', commas after company names, 'Qt Toolkit'), and also on garbled or mis-encoded CJK byte tokens. Ordinary prose barely activates it.

Fires mainly on key words in open-source license boilerplate: 'License', '"AS IS" BASIS', 'binary form', 'copyright notice', 'Version 2.0', 'License at'. Weaker triggers are other formal or legal text, such as 'et al.' and party names in court filings. The license context is what drives it.

Fires on words about recent change or change over time: ' recent' in 'in recent years', ' new', ' increasingly', 'ization', 'ified', ' changed', ' update', ' entered', 'took office', 'now that'. The context describes something that has developed, changed or been newly introduced.

Diffuse. It fires on scattered tokens across code (struct field names, function arguments), math word problems (numbers or variables after operators), biographies (' in', a date's space) and prose words, with no clear shared feature.

Fires on internal subword pieces of non-English, mostly South Asian, Middle Eastern or Central Asian proper names and words: 'As' in Asghar/Asyr, 'Bud' in Budgam, 'az' in Waziristan, 'Gur' in Gurdaspur, 'th' in Pantham. Weaker triggers are other fragmented foreign tokens and date format strings like '%Y'.

Fires on words that express extent, span or range: ' to' in 'from 1938 to 1970', the last digit of year ranges, ' covered' or ' covers' in 'covers the area', ' ended', ' span', ' consisting of'. It also fires on layout extent values in code ('match_parent', 'row-fluid', width or height values).

Fires mainly on the preposition ' in' (also ' on') when it marks a physical location or state after a verb of position or presence: 'waited in line', 'stood in', 'lurk in the shallows', 'was in full swing', 'still on the playa'. Weaker triggers are adjectives describing setting or condition ('in perfect condition', 'spectacular settings').

Fires on the token right after a title-like header ends. Examples are the name of the project in 'This file is part of the X project/Framework' and the double newline after a blog post date line ('February 24, 2018⏎⏎'). Smaller offshoots are include-guard names and language names ('C++', 'C#').
Fires on the word 'two' (and 'Two') used as a quantifier, especially in 'these two', 'the other two', 'any two', 'into two kinds'. It fires much more weakly on the digit '2' inside numbers.

Fires on tokens at the start of code files, in import, include and doctype lines: '.app' and '.util' in 'import android.app', '.h' in '#include <stdlib.h>', '<html' after '<!DOCTYPE html>', '#['. Weaker triggers are scattered subword pieces of names.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word split into several tokens, often a rare technical or medical term (' pem'phigus, 'exam'ethyl, ' polym'orphonuclear, ' par'affin, ' att'ested, ' dem'arcation). The unit seems to predict how the word continues.
